ramanuja.summary: Answered Shankara with a qualified non-dualism in which the world and individual selves are real as the body of the divine, opening devotion to those outside the upper castes.

seljuk-empire.summary: Turkic dynasty out of the steppe that took Baghdad, shattered Byzantine power at Manzikert in 1071, and so opened Anatolia to Turkish settlement and Europe to the idea of a crusade.

magnetic-compass.summary: Known as a divination tool earlier, described for navigation by the eleventh century — the instrument that made open-ocean sailing routine.

movable-type.summary: Bi Sheng cut individual characters in clay four centuries before Gutenberg. With tens of thousands of characters to handle, it never displaced woodblock printing in China the way it did in Europe.

cahokia.summary: The largest city north of Mexico before the eighteenth century, centred on an earthen mound with a larger base than the Great Pyramid, and abandoned before any European saw it.

al-ghazali.summary: Attacked the claims of the philosophers on their own logical terms, then turned to Sufism, reshaping Islamic thought for centuries.

khwarazmian-empire.summary: The dominant power of Central Asia until its shah executed Genghis Khan's envoys, an error that brought the Mongols down on it and erased the state within five years.

great-zimbabwe.summary: A capital of dry-stone walls up to eleven metres high, at the centre of a gold-trading state linked to the Swahili coast and the Indian Ocean.
great-zimbabwe.note: Colonial-era officials insisted the stonework could not be African and suppressed evidence to the contrary; its Shona origin is not in doubt.

timbuktu.summary: A Saharan trading city that became a centre of Islamic scholarship, its manuscript libraries holding works on astronomy, law and medicine — evidence of a written African intellectual tradition that colonial historiography denied existed.

angkor-wat.summary: The largest religious structure ever built, raised as a Hindu temple to Vishnu and later becoming Buddhist — and never wholly abandoned.

bhaskara-ii.summary: Wrote the Siddhanta Shiromani, handling quadratic and indeterminate equations and anticipating parts of differential calculus.

ibn-rushd.summary: Defended philosophy against al-Ghazali and wrote commentaries on Aristotle that carried Greek thought back into Latin Europe.

iroquois-confederacy.summary: A league of five, later six, nations governed by a recorded constitution with councils, consensus procedure and the power of clan mothers to remove leaders — one of the longest-running participatory systems anywhere.
iroquois-confederacy.note: Oral tradition and a solar eclipse point to 1142; many historians prefer the fifteenth century. Claims about its influence on the US constitution are debated but were formally acknowledged by Congress in 1988.

settlement-of-rapa-nui.summary: The easternmost point of Polynesian settlement, reached across some of the emptiest ocean on the planet.

genghis-khan.summary: Unified the Mongol tribes and built, in twenty years, the machinery that would conquer more territory than any leader before or since.
genghis-khan.note: The birth year is given variously as 1155, 1162 or 1167 across the surviving sources.

benin-kingdom.summary: A West African state renowned for brass and ivory sculpture of extraordinary technical refinement, sacked by a British expedition in 1897 whose loot is still held in museums across Europe and North America.

kamakura-shogunate.summary: Military government under the shogun, with the emperor reduced to ceremony. It twice survived Mongol invasion, helped by the storms later called kamikaze.

madhvacharya.summary: Argued for outright dualism, holding the difference between God, self and world to be permanent and real.

delhi-sultanate.summary: Five successive Muslim dynasties ruling from Delhi, which repelled the Mongols, extended briefly over most of the subcontinent, and fell to Babur at Panipat.

mongol-empire.summary: The largest contiguous land empire in history, stretching from Korea to Hungary. Its conquests were catastrophically violent, and the peace that followed moved goods, technologies, people and plague across Eurasia faster than at any time before.
mongol-empire.note: Mortality estimates for the conquests run to tens of millions and are built largely from chroniclers with reason to exaggerate.

aquinas.summary: Reconciled Aristotle with Christian theology so thoroughly that the synthesis became Catholic orthodoxy.

chagatai-khanate.summary: The Mongol successor state in Central Asia proper, from which Timur and later Babur both drew their legitimacy.

mali-empire.summary: West African empire controlling the trans-Saharan gold trade, whose ruler Mansa Musa made Timbuktu a centre of scholarship.

golden-horde.summary: The Mongol successor state over the Russian principalities, whose two and a half centuries of overlordship shaped the autocratic state that Moscow became after throwing it off.

moai.summary: Nearly a thousand monolithic ancestor figures, the largest almost ten metres tall, carved from volcanic tuff and moved kilometres across the island without draught animals or wheels.

settlement-of-aotearoa.summary: The last major landmass on Earth to be settled by humans, reached by Polynesian voyagers who became the Māori.

sack-of-baghdad.summary: Ended the Abbasid Caliphate and destroyed the House of Wisdom with its libraries, a loss from which the Islamic scholarly world took centuries to recover.

ethiopian-empire.summary: Seven centuries of continuous statehood, the only African power to defeat a European army decisively at Adwa in 1896 and so escape the partition of the continent.

yuan-dynasty.summary: Mongol rule over all of China, which opened the overland routes wide enough for Marco Polo to travel them and for plague to travel back.

majapahit.summary: The last major Hindu-Buddhist empire of the archipelago, whose claimed reach across maritime Southeast Asia is still invoked in Indonesian national memory.

ottoman-empire.summary: Six centuries of rule from Anatolia across the Balkans, the Levant and North Africa, ending the Byzantine empire at Constantinople in 1453.

oyo-empire.summary: A Yoruba state whose cavalry dominated the forest belt, governed through a council that could compel a king to take his own life.

renaissance.summary: A revival of classical learning and naturalistic art beginning in the Italian city-states and spreading across Europe.

timur.summary: Conqueror from Transoxiana who campaigned from Delhi to Ankara with exceptional brutality, and spent the proceeds making Samarkand one of the most beautiful cities on Earth.

mansa-musa-hajj.summary: The Mali emperor crossed the Sahara with an entourage so laden with gold that his spending in Cairo is said to have depressed its value for a decade, and put Mali on European maps for the first time.

tenochtitlan.summary: Built on an island in Lake Texcoco and grown by floating gardens and causeways into a city of perhaps two hundred thousand — larger than any in Spain when the Spanish arrived.

ibn-khaldun.summary: Treated the rise and fall of states as a subject with its own laws, founding something close to sociology four centuries early.

vijayanagara-empire.summary: South Indian empire centred on Hampi, which checked sultanate expansion southward for two centuries until its defeat at Talikota in 1565.

black-death.summary: The deadliest documented pandemic, which reached Europe along trade routes from Central Asia and killed so large a share of the population that wages rose, serfdom weakened, and the social order did not recover its former shape.
black-death.note: Estimates run from 30% to 60% of Europe's population; the figure varies enormously by region and the records are uneven.

second-plague-pandemic.summary: The Black Death was the opening wave of an era of recurring plague outbreaks that returned somewhere in Europe or the Mediterranean roughly every decade for five centuries.

ayutthaya.summary: A cosmopolitan Siamese capital that hosted Portuguese, Dutch, Japanese and Persian quarters, and was destroyed by a Burmese army after four centuries.

ming-dynasty.summary: Restored native Chinese rule after the Mongol Yuan; built the Forbidden City and sent Zheng He's treasure fleets across the Indian Ocean.

timurid-empire.summary: Presided over a renaissance in Persian painting, architecture and astronomy; its displaced heir Babur went on to found the Mughal Empire in India.

joseon-dynasty.summary: Five centuries of Confucian rule, and the origin of hangul — an alphabet designed from scratch in the 1440s to be learnable in a morning, explicitly so that commoners could write.

ulugh-beg.summary: A Timurid ruler who built a three-storey sextant at Samarkand and catalogued nearly a thousand stars to an accuracy unmatched until the telescope — then was murdered by his son for his trouble.

kabir.summary: Weaver and poet-saint of Varanasi whose blunt couplets rejected both Hindu and Islamic orthodoxy in favour of direct, imageless devotion. Verses attributed to him appear in the Sikh Guru Granth Sahib.
kabir.note: Traditional accounts give 1398–1518, a span of 120 years; most modern scholars prefer c. 1440–1518. The hagiographies are late and the poems were transmitted orally before being collected.

zheng-he-voyages.summary: Seven Ming treasure fleets reached India, Arabia and East Africa with ships far larger than anything in Europe — and were then halted by imperial decree, the records burned, decades before Columbus sailed.

aztec-empire.summary: A tribute empire of the Triple Alliance dominating central Mexico, with compulsory schooling, botanical gardens and a professional merchant class — brought down in two years by disease, Spanish steel and the tens of thousands of subject-city allies who joined the invaders.

inca-empire.summary: The largest pre-Columbian state, administered without writing or the wheel through quipu records and a road network spanning the Andes.

printing-press.summary: Movable metal type in Mainz made books reproducible at scale, accelerating the Reformation, the scientific revolution and mass literacy.

hangul.summary: One of the very few writing systems with a known inventor, a known date and a stated rationale — its letter shapes depict the mouth positions that make the sounds.

songhai-empire.summary: The largest state in West African history at its height, ended by a Moroccan army carrying firearms across the Sahara.

sengoku-period.summary: A century and a half of warring domains, ended by three successive unifiers and the firearms Portuguese traders had introduced.

guru-nanak.summary: Founder of Sikhism, whose teaching of one formless God and rejection of caste and ritual drew on and reshaped the Bhakti and Sufi currents of his time.

copernicus.summary: Put the Sun rather than the Earth at the centre of the planetary system, published as he lay dying.

columbian-exchange-epidemics.summary: Smallpox, measles, influenza and typhus arrived with Europeans in populations with no prior exposure, causing the largest demographic catastrophe in recorded history and enabling conquests that force alone could not have achieved.
columbian-exchange-epidemics.note: Estimates of indigenous population loss range from about 50% to over 90% across the Americas. The pre-contact population itself is disputed, which is why the proportion is uncertain rather than the death toll alone.

sources.title: Smithsonian — Disease and the Columbian Exchange

columbus-1492.summary: Four voyages looking for Asia, which instead began the permanent linking of two hemispheres — and, within a generation, the collapse of the Caribbean's indigenous population.

tulsidas.summary: Poet-saint who composed the Ramcharitmanas, retelling the Ramayana in Awadhi rather than Sanskrit and so placing the story of Rama in the mouths of ordinary people across North India.
tulsidas.note: Birth year is disputed between 1497, 1511 and 1532; 1511 is the most commonly cited. The death year of 1623 is better attested.

mirabai.summary: Rajput princess turned wandering devotee of Krishna, whose bhajans in Rajasthani and Braj remain among the most widely sung devotional poems in India.
mirabai.note: Dates rest entirely on later hagiography; nothing contemporary survives.
